transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-01 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Derek (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Ember CTO), Ana Gomez (SRE), Priya Kumar (ML Eng), Tom Reeves (Infra)

Summary (auto): Deep technical deep-dive on tail latency (p95/p99). Focus on runtime knobs, batching, kv cache, and network topology impacts. Action items and benchmarks agreed.

[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I'm Samira, AE on the account, and with me are Derek and Lena from our SE team.
[00:12] Marcus (Ember CTO): Hey Samira, hi team. We're excited; p99 has been a thorn for us, especially afternoon peaks.
[00:20] Derek (Redwood SE): Cool, can I kick us off with the goals? We want to understand your current p95/p99 baseline, workload characteristics, and where the major network or runtime hops are. Also validate streaming vs non-streaming behavior.
[00:33] Ana (SRE): Sounds good. For context, we run a multi-tenant app on GCP and in prod we see p95 around 180ms and p99 spikes to 1.2s on shorter prompts, and worse for longer sessions. That varies by model size and whether streaming is on.
[00:48] Priya (ML): Our typical prompts are 40-80 tokens, but a lot of multi-turn context pushes KV cache sizes. We also do on-the-fly reranking for top-k which increases token generation.

[01:15] Derek (Redwood SE): Okay let's unpack. First, streaming vs non-streaming: streaming adds some overhead due to chunking and flush intervals, but it can lower perceived latency for users because they get tokens earlier. Non-streaming tends to batch better but the end-to-end latency for p99 can be dominated by tail token generation and scheduling.
[01:45] Marcus: We saw streaming helped UX but made p99 worse during bursts. We think there's network serialization or extra hops with our CDN.
[02:05] Lena (Redwood SE): Right, there's often a tradeoff: streaming increases number of network packets and head-of-line blocking in some proxies. Also, if your fronting layer aggregates streams, that can add queuing.

[02:40] Tom (Infra): Our infra does an L7 proxy plus an internal API gateway, then VPC peering to the Redwood Dedicated endpoint for the pilot. That adds 2x network hops. Could that explain the tail?
[03:00] Derek: Absolutely, network hops + small packet bursts can inflate p99. Also variable serialization delays on the gateway can cause jitter. For p99 we typically instrument at three points: client-to-edge, edge-to-runtime, and runtime internal queues.
[03:25] Ana: We have traces but they're noisy. What instrumentation do you recommend?
[03:33] Derek: We'll share a lightweight tracing snippet - we'll show exact headers to capture request arrival, scheduler dequeue, model start, token emit times. That helps separate network vs runtime.

[04:10] Priya: Let's talk KV cache. We see cold-starts when requests hit different workers. p99 jumps when the KV cache is cold and the model has to refill.
[04:25] Derek: That's common. Two things: shard affinity and warm routing. If your routing spreads requests across workers indiscriminately, cache misses will kill you. You can use sticky routing or a consistent hashing layer to keep a user's session on a worker so KV cache hit rate improves.
[04:50] Marcus: Is that something Redwood handles in the routing layer or do we need to change our client?
[04:58] Lena: Our smart routing can do affinity based on session id or prefix; however that comes with throughput tradeoffs. We'll show config options.

[05:30] Samira: Also batching - how big are your requests when you batch? What's your arrival pattern?
[05:38] Ana: During peaks we get bursts of small requests, 5-20 concurrent requests per worker. We tried batch size 8 and 16, but saw latency regresses for short prompts.
[05:52] Derek: Yeah batching increases GPU utilization but can increase tail latency for short requests if you wait to fill batches. Continuous batching with a max wait threshold (like 5ms to 20ms) often helps. Also hybrid batching: prioritize small-median requests to avoid head-of-line for tiny prompts.

[06:28] Priya: What about dynamic batching and KV cache interactions?
[06:35] Derek: If you batch across different sessions that have different KV states, you still benefit from shared computation in the attention kernels, but you need to ensure cache reads are efficient. For transformers the KV read is per-token and per-head; if the kernel memory layout is not cache-friendly, that adds CPU/GPU overhead.
[07:00] Marcus: Any quick wins we can try before a pilot?
[07:05] Derek: Yes: enable sticky routing for high-value sessions, reduce batch max wait to 5ms for short prompts, enable prefix caching for repeated prompts, and instrument model start / first-token times.

[07:40] Ana: We heard about quantization improving throughput but sometimes increasing p99 due to dequant/dequantization steps. Experience?
[07:48] Lena: Good point. Quantization (8-bit/4-bit) reduces token latency on some kernels but can also add dequant overhead, depending on the runtime path. For small sequence lengths the quant overhead can dominate. We recommend benchmarking 8-bit per workload; 4-bit is great for throughput but you must measure tail behavior.
[08:10] Derek: Also mixing: run critical paths in fp16 and bulk in int8 where possible. The runtime will pick kernels - we can share kernel selection heuristics used in our compiler.

[08:45] Marcus: Network hops - how much latency should we expect from VPC peering + proxies?
[08:52] Derek: Usually 1-3 ms per hop in-region, but proxy queuing and retries add more. For p99 it's less about raw RTT and more queue/serialization variance. If you cross regions or go through a managed gateway, that can add 20-50ms occasionally.
[09:15] Tom: We're considering on-prem for data-sensitivity. How different is tail behavior on Private (on-prem) compared to hosted?
[09:24] Lena: On-prem removes public network variation, but you inherit local network topology and your own proxies. If you colocate model runtime close to clients, p99 can improve. But hardware variability (noisy neighbors on GPU clusters) can still cause spikes.

[10:00] Priya: Any recommendations for avoiding noisy neighbors?
[10:05] Derek: Dedicated pools (reservation) with pinned instances are best. If you're on shared pools, use scheduling windows and CPU/GPU isolation or reserved capacity. Redwood Dedicated offers reserved pools with guaranteed throughput.

[10:38] Marcus: Can we do a short walkthrough of a sample benchmark?
[10:45] Derek: Sure. I have a benchmark summary from a recent customer. For a 7B model with sticky routing and continuous batching (5ms max wait) we saw p95 at ~90ms and p99 at ~180-220ms in-hosted region. Without sticky routing p99 ballooned to 800-1200ms due to cold KV misses.
[11:10] Samira: I'll drop that spreadsheet in the notes - link to benchmark sheet (redwood.com/benchmarks/mock-sheet) - it's a placeholder but similar numbers.

[11:35] Ana: On our side, we saw p99 correlated with background jobs - backups and periodic autoscaling events. Does Redwood have guards against background eviction?
[11:45] Lena: At the runtime we try to minimize host-level preemption; for Dedicated pools we provide isolation. For hosted, we do soft eviction and can migrate sessions with preserved state, but that has tail implications.

[12:15] Derek: A note on streaming: if you stream partial tokens and your client concatenates, you'll see earlier first-byte latency but sometimes longer final-token p99 due to retransmits and small flush windows. We recommend measuring both first-byte and end-to-end token times.

[12:48] Priya: Are there specific metrics we should add to our dashboards?
[12:52] Derek: Yes: request arrival time, scheduler enqueue/dequeue, model start, first-token emitted, last-token emitted, batch size distribution, KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization percentiles, and network hop latencies.

[13:20] Marcus: About reranking - does doing reranks in-line affect p99 much?
[13:27] Derek: If reranking is synchronous, yes. Each additional model call multiplies tail exposure. Consider async reranking or precomputing candidate embeddings. For p99-sensitive flows, we sometimes do partial ranking on the same response and full ranking in background with eventual refinement.

[13:55] Tom: Any thoughts on kernel selection and sequence lengths?
[14:00] Lena: Kernels are tuned by sequence length and batch shape. If you have varied sequence lengths in a batch, the runtime may pad to the max, increasing compute for short ones. Grouping by similar sequence length can improve efficiency and reduce tail.

[14:30] Priya: For our use-case, most requests are 40-80 tokens, but occasionally a few are 300 tokens. We see p99 spikes when long sequences intermix.
[14:40] Derek: Try length bucketing at the scheduler and prioritize short-run buckets for interactive traffic. Also consider preemptive scheduling where long jobs yield GPU time slices.

[15:05] Marcus: Let's talk about concrete experiment steps.
[15:12] Samira: Agreed. We'll run two experiments: 1) Sticky routing + small max wait (5ms) + continuous batching; 2) No sticky routing + longer max wait (20ms) but higher batch sizes. We'll compare p50/p95/p99 and first-byte times.
[15:30] Derek: We'll provide an instrumentation snippet to tag traces with session id and batch id. Please include your trace sample so we can align.

[15:55] Ana: About security/compliance - if we go Dedicated or Private, what about KMS integration and audit logs?
[16:02] Samira: Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM and audit logging. We'll also share our SOC 2 and ISO summaries. I'll attach the security deck.

[16:25] Priya: The team also asked about fallbacks - if a worker fails mid-session what's the impact on KV cache and latency?
[16:33] Derek: We support automatic fallback to a compatible model variant; however KV cache won't be preserved across workers unless you have shared external KV. That introduces a cold cache. For stateful high-SLO flows we recommend sticky routing plus a small external session store for essential context, or dedicating capacity.

[17:05] Marcus: Is there any roadmap feature we should know that helps p99?
[17:10] Lena: We're working on global KV-sharing for session hotness and faster reheating, plus more advanced pre-warming heuristics. Not GA but available in pilot for some customers.

[17:40] Derek: For quantization: run microbenchmarks - 8-bit often gives best latency for medium models. But for tail-sensitive production interactive apps you should validate first-token latency.

[18:05] Priya: On custom models - we plan to tune our fine-tuned 7B. Anything special there?
[18:12] Derek: Fine-tuned weights sometimes shift kernel perf; always run a short perf sweep. Also check KV size growth for longer contexts.

[18:40] Samira: Quick recap: Redwood to share benchmark sheet, tracing snippet, security deck. Ember to send 1k trace samples plus example prompt distribution. We'll schedule pilot kickoff after we review traces.

[19:00] Marcus: Sounds good. A couple of smaller questions - any quick tips around CDN or edge?
[19:06] Lena: Keep edge layers simple for streaming. Avoid aggregating streams at the edge where possible. Also TLS termination location matters for early data.

[19:35] Ana: One last thing - our autoscaler causes small VM churn; any suggestions?
[19:40] Derek: Try slower scale-down cooldowns for frontends and use draining hooks to preserve in-flight sessions; also consider warm pool of workers so you reduce cold-starts.

[20:05] Priya: Are you able to run a synthetic p99 replay in Redwood infra with our traces?
[20:10] Derek: Yes, if you provide traces and model config we can run a replay to emulate tail conditions and measure p95/p99. We'll include streaming/non-streaming modes.

[20:35] Samira: Ok we'll aim to get the traces and schedule the replay. Anything else?
[20:40] Marcus: No that's it from us. Appreciate the level of detail.

[20:50] Samira: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and next steps.

[58:00] Meeting end.
